body: Mosul spreads across both banks of the Tigris, with broad newer roads, concrete apartment blocks, shopfronts with Arabic signs, and older limestone and brick buildings nearer the west bank. The river moves steadily beneath its bridges; traffic sounds are horns, engines, and vendors calling from busy markets. Al-Hadba minaret and the restored al-Nuri mosque mark the old skyline. The Iraqi flag has horizontal red, white, and black stripes, with green Kufic الله أكبر centered on the white stripe. Summers are bright and dry; winter light is cooler. People wear everyday shirts, jeans, abayas, and headscarves, greeting one another with «السلام عليكم» and «شلونك؟».

topic: Mosul old city and the al-Nuri mosque
body: Mosul’s old city has close-set limestone and brick houses, narrow winding lanes, recessed doorways, and small shops with Arabic signs. At the restored al-Nuri mosque, pale stone surfaces and the rebuilt Al-Hadba minaret stand above low rooftops; the minaret retains its characteristic lean. Footsteps and conversation carry through the lanes, while motorcycles pass slowly where there is room. Strong summer sun makes sharp shadows under arches and balconies. The Iraqi flag has horizontal red, white, and black stripes, with green Kufic الله أكبر centered on white. Residents and visitors wear ordinary city clothes, abayas, or headscarves and say «السلام عليكم» or «شلونك؟».

Kirkuk’s citadel rises on a broad earthen mound above crowded streets, its weathered brick and plaster walls visible beyond shop signs in Arabic and Kurdish. Below it are market lanes, concrete storefronts, traffic circles, and low-rise neighborhoods; farther out, the city opens toward flat plains. Cars, market calls, and footsteps make a layered street sound. The Iraqi flag has horizontal red, white, and black stripes, with green Kufic الله أكبر centered on white. Sunlight is harsh in summer and soft on dusty winter afternoons. People wear shirts, jeans, headscarves, abayas, or Kurdish dress; greetings include Arabic «السلام عليكم» and Kurdish «سڵاو، چۆنی؟».

Duhok fills a valley between dry, folded mountains. Its streets mix concrete apartment buildings, stone-faced shops, Kurdish and Arabic signs, roadside trees, and busy cafés; the Duhok Dam lies against the hills beyond the center. Cars climb and descend the valley roads, while café conversation and traffic carry through warm evenings. The Kurdistan Region flag has horizontal red, white, and green stripes, with a yellow sun of 21 rays centered on white. Summer light is strong and dry; mountain winters are cooler. People wear modern everyday clothes, long dresses and headscarves, or Kurdish shalwar with a waist sash. A common greeting is «سڵاو، چۆنی؟».

Zakho’s Delal Bridge crosses the Khabur River in pale, rough-cut stone. Its tall central arch and smaller openings throw dark reflections onto the moving water; uneven stonework catches warm light near sunset. The surrounding town has low concrete and stone buildings, Kurdish and Arabic shop signs, riverside paths, and mountain slopes in the distance. Water runs softly beneath the bridge while nearby roads bring engine noise and conversation. The Kurdistan Region flag has horizontal red, white, and green stripes, with a yellow 21-ray sun centered on white. People wear everyday clothes or Kurdish dress and greet friends with «سڵاو، چۆنی؟».

Amadiya sits on a steep-sided, flat-topped mountain above green valleys and surrounding ridges. From a distance its houses form a compact strip along the plateau; inside are narrow streets, stone walls, concrete buildings, small shops, and signs in Kurdish and Arabic. The old stone gate marks a historic approach to the town. Footsteps and voices sound close in the lanes, while wind is more noticeable at the exposed edges. The Kurdistan Region flag has horizontal red, white, and green stripes, with a yellow sun of 21 rays centered on white. Winters can be cold; people wear jackets, headscarves, or Kurdish dress and say «سڵاو، چۆنی؟».

Halabja lies among cultivated fields and foothills near the Iranian border. Its streets have low concrete buildings, modest shopfronts with Kurdish and Arabic lettering, planted medians, and views toward layered mountains. Orchards and fields turn green in spring; summer sun is bright, while winter can bring rain and cold. Cars and motorcycles pass at an ordinary town pace, with voices outside shops and birds audible in quieter areas. The Kurdistan Region flag has horizontal red, white, and green stripes, with a yellow 21-ray sun centered on white. Residents wear everyday coats or shirts, headscarves, long dresses, and Kurdish dress; they greet one another with «سڵاو، چۆنی؟».

Ranya has low-rise concrete buildings, Kurdish and Arabic shop signs, busy market streets, and hills rising beyond town. Nearby Lake Dukan spreads through a wide mountain basin: blue-green water, irregular rocky shores, and pale slopes change shape with the reservoir’s water level. Small boats leave spreading wakes; along the shore, wind ripples the surface and carries voices from visitors. Clear summer sun produces hard shadows, while cooler seasons soften the distant hills. The Kurdistan Region flag has horizontal red, white, and green stripes, with a yellow sun of 21 rays centered on white. People wear everyday clothes or Kurdish dress and greet each other with «سڵاو، چۆنی؟».

Soran sits among steep, pale limestone mountains in the Kurdistan Region. The Hamilton Road winds out of town on narrow asphalt bends, passing rock-cut sections, short tunnels and barriers above deep valleys. Cars slow for sharp turns; tyres hiss on wet pavement and engines echo between cliffs. In town, concrete shopfronts carry Kurdish and Arabic signs, and people wear everyday shirts, trousers, dresses or Kurdish traditional clothing. The Kurdistan flag has horizontal red, white and green bands with a yellow 21-rayed sun centred on the white band. Iraq’s flag has red, white and black bands, with green Arabic «الله أكبر» centred on white. Greetings include «سڵاو، چۆنی؟» and the respectful address «کاک».

Rawanduz canyon drops sharply below the town: massive grey and tan rock walls frame a narrow river and patches of green vegetation far beneath the rim. From viewpoints, buildings appear close to the cliff edge; roads curve around the mountains rather than crossing the open drop. Wind is audible on exposed ledges, while moving water sounds faint from above. Summer light is hard and clear, revealing layered stone; winter can bring mist or snow. Visitors wear ordinary jackets or casual clothes and speak Sorani Kurdish, greeting each other with «سڵاو» and addressing men politely as «کاک». The Kurdistan flag is red, white and green horizontally, with a yellow 21-rayed sun centred on white; Iraq’s is red, white and black with green «الله أكبر» on white.

Akre’s older neighbourhood climbs a steep hillside in tiers of close-set stone and plaster houses, narrow lanes and steps, with mountains rising behind it. Lower streets have newer concrete shops and Kurdish and Arabic signs; cars move slowly where pedestrians cross. At Newroz, torchlights can trace the hillside after dark, their flames flickering in the wind. In daylight, pale walls reflect strong sun; evenings cool quickly. People wear everyday clothes or colourful Kurdish dress and greet one another with «سڵاو، چۆنی؟», often using «کاک» as a respectful address. The Kurdistan flag has horizontal red, white and green bands and a centred yellow 21-rayed sun. Iraq’s flag is red, white and black, with green «الله أكبر» centred on white.

Shaqlawa lies below the broad slopes of Mount Safeen. Its streets mix concrete hotels and shops with fruit stalls, cafés and Kurdish and Arabic signs; orchards and wooded slopes sit beyond the built-up centre. Market awnings throw shade over displays of pomegranates, nuts and honey. Cars pass at a modest pace, voices carry between storefronts, and mountain air can turn cool after a warm afternoon. Residents and visitors wear modern casual clothes, while some wear traditional Kurdish outfits. A common greeting is «سڵاو، چۆنی؟»; «کاک» is a polite form of address. The Kurdistan flag is horizontally red, white and green with a yellow 21-rayed sun centred on white. Iraq’s red-white-black flag bears green «الله أكبر» on its white band.

Penjwen is a mountain town near Iraq’s border with Iran, with low concrete buildings, Kurdish shop signs and roads leading past fields into rugged hills. The landscape is green in wetter months, dusty in dry weather and often snow-covered in winter. Wind moves across exposed ground; traffic and conversations are concentrated along the main streets. People dress for the season in coats, everyday clothes or Kurdish traditional clothing. Sorani greetings include «سڵاو» and «چۆنی؟», with «کاک» used respectfully. The Kurdistan flag has red, white and green horizontal bands and a yellow 21-rayed sun centred on white. Iraq’s flag has horizontal red, white and black bands with green Arabic «الله أكبر» centred on the white band.

Tikrit stands above the Tigris, with broad roads, low-rise concrete and brick buildings, Arabic shop signs and stretches of palms and cultivated riverbank. The river moves steadily beneath bridges, reflecting pale sky and the warmer tones of late-afternoon light. Traffic brings engine noise and horns; quieter streets carry voices from cafés and shops. Summers are hot and bright, while winter mornings can be cool. People commonly wear shirts, trousers, abayas or dishdashas. Greetings include «السلام عليكم» and Iraqi Arabic «شلونك؟»; «أستاذ» and «حجي» can be respectful forms of address. Iraq’s flag has three horizontal bands—red, white and black—with green Arabic «الله أكبر» centred on the white band.

Samarra’s Malwiya rises beside the vast, roofless Great Mosque enclosure: a tall, tapering baked-brick tower wrapped by one broad exterior spiral ramp, not a narrow internal staircase. Its sandy brown masonry stands against a wide, bright sky; footsteps and wind sound distinct in the open space. Elsewhere in the city, the golden dome and minarets of the Al-Askari shrine form a separate landmark among streets of concrete and brick with Arabic signs. People wear everyday clothes, abayas or dishdashas and greet one another with «السلام عليكم» or «شلونك؟», sometimes addressing someone as «أستاذ». Iraq’s flag is horizontally red, white and black, with green Arabic «الله أكبر» centred on white.

Baqubah’s streets run through low-rise concrete and brick neighbourhoods toward the Diyala River and surrounding orchards. Arabic shop signs, roadside produce stands, palms and citrus trees give the city a greener edge than the dry open ground beyond it. In strong summer sun, awnings shade pedestrians and fruit; irrigation water moves slowly through channels, while cars, motorcycles and market voices supply the street sound. People wear ordinary shirts and trousers, abayas or dishdashas. Common greetings are «السلام عليكم» and Iraqi «شلونك؟», with «أستاذ» or «حجي» used respectfully. Iraq’s flag has horizontal red, white and black bands, with green Arabic «الله أكبر» centred on the white band.

Kut curves around the Tigris in Wasit province. Along the riverfront, concrete embankments face brown-green water, low shopfronts, apartment blocks and the pale structure of the Kut Barrage. Arabic signs read مطعم or صيدلية; yellow taxis and motorcycles move through busy market streets. Date palms break the flat skyline. In summer, hard sunlight washes the buildings beige; river breezes stir awnings and carry traffic noise and calls from vendors. Iraqi flags are red, white and black horizontal bands with green الله أكبر in Kufic script centered on the white. People wear shirts, trousers, abayas or dishdashas, greeting one another with هلا والله and شلونك؟

Amarah sits beside the Tigris in Maysan. Its riverfront has concrete railings, riverside cafés and bridges over slow brown water; beyond them are dense streets of cream concrete buildings, Arabic shop signs and shaded market stalls. The surrounding land is flat, with palms and waterways leading toward the marshes, not reed houses filling the city centre. In hot, hazy light, ceiling fans turn in open-front shops while motorcycles, taxis and conversation make a steady street sound. The Iraqi flag has red, white and black horizontal bands and green Kufic الله أكبر on the white. Residents in everyday clothes, abayas and dishdashas say هلا بيك and شلونك؟

Nasiriyah stands on the Euphrates in Dhi Qar. Around Al-Habboubi Square, cars circle past shops with Arabic lettering, concrete façades and the square’s monument; busier streets run toward river bridges and low palm-lined banks. The city is mostly flat, its pale buildings sharp-edged under intense summer sun and softened by dust at dusk. Water moves slowly beneath bridges while horns, engines and market voices overlap. Iraqi flags show red, white and black horizontal stripes, with green Kufic الله أكبر centered in the white stripe. People in shirts and trousers, abayas or dishdashas greet friends with هلا والله, شلونك؟ and the respectful address حجي.

At Ur near Nasiriyah, the ziggurat rises from a broad, nearly level plain of pale dust and scattered ancient walls. Its enormous stepped mass has sloping baked-brick faces over a mud-brick core; three steep stairways meet at a landing. The surviving structure is incomplete, not a fully intact tower. Close views show weathered brick joints and reconstructed sections with cleaner edges. Strong sun casts dark triangular shadows under the stairs, while wind pushes dust across the ground. Visitors appear small against the brickwork, walking rather than climbing unrestricted areas. Footsteps crunch on grit; otherwise the site is quiet apart from wind and distant voices.

Samawah follows the Euphrates in Al-Muthanna province, where a ribbon of palms and riverside buildings cuts through a dry, open landscape. Its centre has concrete shopfronts, Arabic signs, small bridges and streets shared by taxis, pickup trucks and motorcycles. The river is broad and slow, reflecting cream walls and a bright, often cloudless sky. In summer, heat shimmers above asphalt; traffic hum, shopkeepers’ voices and water slapping the bank carry along the corniche. The Iraqi flag has horizontal red, white and black bands, with green Kufic الله أكبر centered on white. Residents wear everyday shirts, abayas and dishdashas, saying هلا بيك or شلونك؟

Diwaniyah is a low-rise city beside Shatt al-Diwaniyah, a branch of the Euphrates. Its riverbanks have concrete edges and bridges; nearby streets are lined with beige buildings, Arabic-signed pharmacies, food shops and market stalls under fabric awnings. Cars and motorcycles thread between pedestrians, and palms rise behind the roofs. Summer light is stark, while evenings bring softer gold onto the water. Expect engines, vendors and the scrape of shutters, not the sound of a vast open river. Iraqi flags have red, white and black horizontal bands with green Kufic الله أكبر centered on white. People wear shirts, trousers, abayas or dishdashas and say هلا والله, شلونك؟

Hillah runs along Shatt al-Hillah, a Euphrates branch in Babil province. Bridges connect crowded streets of tan concrete buildings, small balconies, Arabic-signed shops and shaded stalls. Palms and planted riverbanks soften the centre; Babylon’s ruins lie outside town, not among its everyday shopfronts. Under bright sun, cars, motorcycles and pedestrians move around one another while water slides slowly below the bridges. Horns and market voices carry across the river at dusk. Iraqi flags are horizontal red, white and black, with green Kufic الله أكبر centered in the white band. Locals in shirts, abayas or dishdashas greet one another with هلا بيك and شلونك؟

The Babylon archaeological site near Hillah spreads across flat, dusty ground beside the Euphrates. Excavated foundations and partly reconstructed tan brick walls form courtyards and passages; some bricks carry stamped cuneiform. Along the Processional Way, brick lion reliefs are visible, and the dark stone Lion of Babylon sculpture stands nearby. Do not show the original blue Ishtar Gate standing intact here: much of it is displayed abroad. A modern palace on a raised mound overlooks parts of the site. Harsh daylight defines each brick edge; visitors walk between walls with gravel crunching underfoot, wind passing through open spaces and only scattered voices.

Kufa lies beside a branch of the Euphrates near Najaf. Low beige brick houses, shopfronts with Arabic signs, and busy streets lead toward the Mosque of Kufa, whose broad courtyard and arcades draw visitors in modest clothing. Men commonly wear shirts and trousers or dishdashas; many women wear abayas and headscarves. The Iraqi flag has three horizontal stripes, red, white, and black, with green Arabic «الله أكبر» centered on the white stripe. Harsh sun makes short shadows at noon; traffic hums and footsteps echo under the arcades. A greeting is «السلام عليكم»; «وعليكم السلام» answers it. People may address an older man as «حجي».

Ramadi is a low-rise city on the Euphrates, with concrete bridges, sandy shoulders, market streets, and rectangular houses of beige block and brick. Arabic shop signs hang above groceries and repair shops; cars, taxis, and small trucks move through wide, sunlit junctions. The river runs slowly past reeds and planted banks, its surface ruffled by wind. The Iraqi flag has horizontal red, white, and black stripes and green Arabic «الله أكبر» centered on white. Summers are bright and dusty. Men wear shirts and trousers or dishdashas; many women wear headscarves. «هلا بيك» is a welcome; «شلونك؟» asks how someone is. An older man may be addressed as «عمي».

Fallujah sits by the Euphrates, where bridges cross a broad, slow brown-green channel. Its streets have pale concrete buildings, flat roofs, Arabic storefront signs, roadside trees, and mosque minarets rising above the blocks. Cars pass over bridge joints with a repeated thump; market lanes carry engine noise and conversation. The Iraqi flag is three horizontal stripes, red over white over black, with green Arabic «الله أكبر» centered on the white. Strong afternoon light picks out dust on walls and leaves. Men wear trousers and shirts or dishdashas; many women wear abayas or headscarves. People say «السلام عليكم» and reply «وعليكم السلام»; «خوية» is a familiar way to address a man.

Haditha stands along the Euphrates amid dry, pale Anbar terrain. Low houses and shops cluster near river roads, with date palms and reeds adding green strips beside the water; the Haditha Dam and its reservoir are upstream, not in the town centre. Arabic signs mark shops, and trucks and cars pass with tyre noise over dusty pavement. The Iraqi flag has horizontal red, white, and black stripes, with green Arabic «الله أكبر» centered on white. Light is sharp and shadows are dark in summer. Men may wear dishdashas or shirts and trousers; many women wear headscarves. Locals greet with «هلا بيك» or «السلام عليكم» and may address an elder as «عمي».

Anah is an Euphrates town in western Iraq, set between pale, stony ground and the river’s green banks. Show the present-day town rather than the old riverside settlement inundated when the upstream reservoir was filled: modest flat-roofed buildings, Arabic shop signs, narrow local streets, palms, and reeds. Water moves steadily against the bank while wind rustles palm fronds; sunlight turns the dry ground cream and ochre. The Iraqi flag has horizontal red, white, and black stripes, with green Arabic «الله أكبر» centered on white. People wear shirts and trousers, dishdashas, abayas, or headscarves. «شلونك؟» means “how are you?”; «حجي» respectfully addresses an older man.

Hit rises beside the Euphrates in western Anbar, with pale masonry, flat-roofed houses, Arabic signs, and palms along the river. Its traditional waterwheels, or «نواعير», are large wooden circles with spokes and containers around their rims. Where one operates, river current turns it slowly; the containers dip, rise dripping, and empty into a raised channel, accompanied by creaks and splashes. Some wheels may stand still, so a view need not show every one turning. The Iraqi flag has red, white, and black horizontal stripes and green Arabic «الله أكبر» centered on white. People wear dishdashas or everyday shirts, trousers, abayas, and headscarves. A greeting is «السلام عليكم»; an elder may be called «عمي».

The road near Rutba crosses western Iraq’s open desert on long stretches of asphalt, with gravel shoulders, low stony ground, and a wide horizon. Heat shimmer can soften distant trucks and Arabic road signs; wind pushes dust close to the ground. Diesel engines and tyre hiss dominate, broken by stops at modest roadside cafés or fuel stations. This is the Iraqi flag: horizontal red, white, and black stripes, with green Arabic «الله أكبر» centered on white. Drivers wear ordinary shirts and trousers, sometimes dishdashas; travellers may cover their heads against sun and dust. At a stop, «هلا بيك» welcomes someone, and «خوية» is a familiar address.

topic: Al-Qurna where the Tigris and Euphrates meet
body: At Al-Qurna, the Tigris and Euphrates meet to form the Shatt al-Arab. The banks are low and green with date palms and reeds; broad, silty water carries small boats, whose wakes spread and slap against the shore. Nearby streets have concrete buildings, market shops, and Arabic signs. Basra’s light is bright and often hazy, with humid summer air. The Iraqi flag has horizontal red, white, and black stripes, with green Arabic «الله أكبر» centered on white. People wear shirts and trousers, dishdashas, abayas, or headscarves. «السلام عليكم» is answered with «وعليكم السلام»; «شلونك؟» asks how someone is, and «حجي» respectfully addresses an older man.

At Iraq’s southern tip, the Faw peninsula is low and flat, with silty banks, tidal water, salt-streaked ground and scattered date palms near settlements. The Shatt al-Arab widens toward the Gulf; small fishing boats rock against muddy edges, while wind pushes dust across roads and rattles palm fronds. Buildings are mostly low concrete or brick, with Arabic shop signs. Light is harsh and hazy in summer. Fishers may wear loose dishdashas or work clothes; others wear everyday shirts, trousers, abayas or headscarves. People say “السلام عليكم” and “هلا بيك,” addressing someone politely as “أستاذ.” An Iraqi flag, when shown, has horizontal red, white and black bands, with green “الله أكبر” in Kufic script centered on white.

Umm Qasr port is a working waterfront of long concrete quays, stacked multicoloured shipping containers, gantry cranes, warehouses and truck lanes. Cargo ships sit high above the quay; cranes lift containers slowly on cables, with engine hum, reversing beeps and metal-on-metal clanks. Arabic signs include “ميناء أم قصر”; road surfaces are dusty, and Gulf light can be glaring through heat haze. Workers wear hard hats and reflective vests alongside everyday shirts and trousers; some visitors wear dishdashas or abayas. Greetings include “السلام عليكم” and “شلونك؟”; “أستاذ” is a polite form of address. An Iraqi flag has horizontal red, white and black bands, with green Kufic “الله أكبر” centered on white.

Zubair, west of Basra, has broad sunlit roads, low concrete houses, older brick walls, shopfront awnings and Arabic signs for groceries and workshops. Around the market, parked cars and small trucks edge past pedestrians; engines, vendors’ calls and the scrape of rolling shutters carry through dry air. Dust softens the afternoon light, and palms appear in courtyards and at the edges of town. Men may wear dishdashas or shirts and trousers; women may wear abayas, headscarves or other everyday clothes. Neighbours say “السلام عليكم,” “هلا بيك” and “شلونك؟,” sometimes addressing an elder as “حجي.” An Iraqi flag has horizontal red, white and black bands, with green Kufic “الله أكبر” centered on white.

In Abu al-Khasib south of Basra, date palms rise in closely spaced rows above narrow irrigation channels and soft, muddy banks. Their rough brown trunks hold arching green fronds; fallen leaves lie beside garden paths and low brick or concrete houses. Water moves slowly through the channels, reflecting broken strips of sky, while fronds hiss in the wind and birds call from the canopy. Arabic signs mark nearby roads and shops. Garden workers may wear dishdashas or practical shirts and trousers; women’s dress varies, including abayas and headscarves. Visitors hear “السلام عليكم,” “هلا بيك” and the respectful “أستاذ.” An Iraqi flag has horizontal red, white and black bands, with green Kufic “الله أكبر” centered on white.

The Chibayish marshes are shallow waterways threaded through tall golden-green reeds under a wide, bright sky. Long, narrow wooden mashoof boats glide low in the water, pushed by a pole or powered by a small motor; their wakes spread gently between reed beds. Water buffalo stand half-submerged or move heavily through the shallows. Reed-built mudhif guesthouses have tall, curved arches and woven surfaces; water laps softly beneath bird calls and motor buzz. People wear dishdashas, shirts and trousers, abayas or headscarves. Greetings include “السلام عليكم,” “هلا بيك” and “شلونك؟” An Iraqi flag has horizontal red, white and black bands, with green Kufic “الله أكبر” centered on white.

Baghdad’s Mansour district has wide paved streets, planted medians, concrete apartment buildings, walled houses, cafés and bright Arabic shop signs. Along 14 Ramadan Street, cars queue beside restaurants and storefronts; Mansour Mall is a large modern shopping building. Air conditioners hum above traffic, and evening headlights catch dust in the warm air. People wear jeans, shirts, dresses, abayas and headscarves in varied combinations. Friends say “هلا بيك” and “شلونك؟”; shop staff often greet customers with “السلام عليكم” or address them as “أستاذ.” An Iraqi flag has horizontal red, white and black bands, with green Kufic “الله أكبر” centered on white.

Adhamiya’s streets lead past closely spaced shops, older brickwork, concrete houses and Arabic signs toward the Abu Hanifa Mosque, recognizable by its large blue-tiled dome and minarets. Around busy junctions, cars slow for pedestrians; vendors’ voices mix with horns and the call to prayer. Near the Tigris, riverside light is softer, while summer afternoons are bright and dusty. Clothing ranges from shirts and trousers to dishdashas, abayas and headscarves. People greet one another with “السلام عليكم” and “هلا بيك,” and may say “شلونك؟” to a neighbour. An Iraqi flag has horizontal red, white and black bands, with green Kufic “الله أكبر” centered on white.

Kadhimiya’s dense streets and covered market lanes lead toward the shrine of Imam Musa al-Kadhim, whose two gold-clad domes and four gold-clad minarets shine above the surrounding roofs. Stone paving fills with steady foot traffic; fabric, prayer beads and food appear beneath Arabic shop signs. Footsteps, merchants’ calls and the call to prayer mingle, while gold surfaces reflect strong afternoon sun. Visitors wear varied everyday clothes, including dishdashas, abayas and headscarves; shoes are removed where required inside the shrine. Greetings include “السلام عليكم,” “هلا بيك” and the respectful “حجي.” An Iraqi flag has horizontal red, white and black bands, with green Kufic “الله أكبر” centered on white.

Zayouna is an eastern Baghdad neighborhood of walled houses, low apartment blocks, shops and cafés. Along al-Rubaie Street, Arabic shop signs and glass-fronted businesses face steady traffic; side streets are quieter, with parked cars beneath palms and dusty shade trees. Cream concrete, beige stone and painted metal gates dominate the view. Cars ease around double-parked vehicles, and generators add a low hum beneath horns and conversation. Summer light is hard and bright, while winter afternoons turn the façades warm gold. People wear everyday shirts, abayas or jeans, and greet neighbors with “هلا” or “شلونك، عيني؟”

Jadriya occupies a green bend of the Tigris in southern central Baghdad. The University of Baghdad campus, broad roads, riverfront cafés and walled homes sit among palms and mature trees. From Jadriya Bridge, the river looks wide and brown-green, with a slow current that wrinkles around piers; traffic crosses with a continuous tire hiss. Concrete walls, pale paving and Arabic signs catch strong midday sun, while evenings soften into amber reflections on the water. Students carry backpacks; café visitors wear casual clothes, abayas or dishdashas. A familiar greeting is “السلام عليكم,” answered “وعليكم السلام”; someone may be addressed as “أستاذ.”

Arasat Street in Karrada runs past restaurants, cafés, shops and older villas behind high boundary walls. Modern glass fronts stand beside beige concrete buildings, with Arabic illuminated signs, parked SUVs and trees breaking up the frontage. Traffic advances in short bursts around cars pulling into curbside spaces; engines, horns and café chatter overlap. In daylight the pale façades glare, while at night storefront lighting and headlights reflect off the road. Customers and workers wear jeans, shirts, abayas or business clothes. At an entrance, a greeting might be “هلا، تفضل,” and a customer may call a worker “أستاذ.”

Palestine Street is a long, busy eastern Baghdad road lined with shops, offices, apartment buildings and side-street entrances. Arabic signs crowd concrete façades; cables, awnings and roadside trees interrupt the straight view down the traffic lanes. Cars, taxis and minibuses accelerate between junctions, then bunch up at crossings, making a shifting bed of horns, engines and vendor calls. Dust softens distant buildings under harsh summer sun; after dark, shop lights and headlights define the street. Pedestrians in casual clothes, abayas and work uniforms move between storefronts. People greet each other with “السلام عليكم” or “شلونك؟” and may say “عيني” when asking a question.

Sadr City spreads across eastern Baghdad in dense, mostly low-rise blocks. Straight main roads such as al-Falah Street feed narrower residential lanes, where concrete houses have flat roofs, metal gates, rooftop water tanks and satellite dishes. Arabic shop signs hang over produce stalls, bakeries and small storefronts. Taxis and minibuses slow for pedestrians and carts; generators, horns, bargaining and children’s voices mingle in the air. Strong sun picks out dust and pale walls, while awnings cast sharp patches of shade. Residents wear everyday Iraqi clothing, including shirts, dishdashas and abayas, and exchange “هلا” or “شلونك، حجي؟”

Bab al-Sharqi is a crowded central Baghdad district beside Tahrir Square and al-Umma Park. Broad traffic approaches meet older shopping streets, where concrete shopfronts, weathered façades and Arabic signs sit close together. Sidewalk stalls display clothes and small household goods beneath fabric shades. Pedestrians thread around parked cars as taxis brake, horns sound and vendors call out prices. Midday sun leaves deep shadow under awnings; evening traffic glints in shop windows. Shoppers and workers wear jeans, shirts, dishdashas and abayas. A vendor may welcome someone with “تفضل، عيني,” while acquaintances exchange “السلام عليكم” and “وعليكم السلام.”

Shorja is a dense trading district in old central Baghdad, with narrow market passages and crowded shops near al-Rasheed Street. Sacks of spices, cartons, stacked tins and household goods fill storefronts beneath awnings and Arabic signs. Handcarts roll over uneven paving while porters steer between shoppers; wheels rattle, traders call prices and metal shutters clank. Sun enters in bright strips between roofs and fabric shades, leaving goods in warm, dusty shadow. Shopkeepers and customers wear practical everyday clothes, dishdashas or abayas. Bargaining begins with greetings such as “السلام عليكم,” and a seller may answer “تفضل، حجي.”

topic: Baghdad Tahrir square and the Freedom monument
body: Tahrir Square is a broad central Baghdad traffic space near the Tigris and Jumhuriya Bridge. Above one edge rises the Freedom Monument: dark bronze human figures and scenes spread across a long, elevated rectangular slab. Traffic circles below amid horns and tire noise; pedestrians cross in groups, and palms and nearby buildings frame the open sky. Where Iraqi flags appear, they have horizontal red, white and black bands, with green Arabic “الله أكبر” centered on the white band. Strong sun throws the sculpted figures into sharp relief. Visitors in everyday clothes greet companions with “هلا” or “شلونك؟”

Zawraa Park spreads across a large green enclosure in Baghdad’s Karkh district, beside the Baghdad Zoo. Palm trees and trimmed lawns break up broad paved walks; amusement rides rise above them, including a Ferris wheel with bright metal spokes. Families gather at benches and snack kiosks, and children move between play areas while ride motors hum and music carries across the paths. Arabic signs mark entrances and attractions. In summer, hard sunlight makes the pavement glare and sends people toward tree shade; after sunset, coloured ride lights stand out against the darkening sky.

Abu Nuwas Street runs beside the Tigris on Baghdad’s Karrada side. Traffic passes a riverside promenade with trees, railings and views across the broad, slow-moving brown water. Open-air restaurants are known for masgouf: fish held upright near wood fires, with smoke drifting above tables and the sound of dishes mixing with traffic. Families stroll near the river, especially in the cooler evening hours. Arabic restaurant signs, concrete kerbs and palms give the street its everyday texture. The water catches gold light at sunset, while bridge lights and reflections appear after dark.

Al-Shaheed Monument stands on an island-like circular platform within a shallow artificial lake in eastern Baghdad. Its immense turquoise-blue tiled dome is split into two offset hemispheres, leaving a tall open gap rather than a complete shell. Broad steps and paved approaches lead toward the water. From a distance, the two curved halves appear almost to meet; as the viewpoint shifts, their separation becomes clear. Sunlight picks out the small tile pattern, and the blue forms reflect in still water. Footsteps carry across the open paving, with city traffic audible beyond the grounds.

The Hands of Victory are two monumental arches spanning the parade road at Baghdad’s Grand Festivities Square. Each arch is formed by enormous crossed metal swords held aloft by sculpted bronze hands rising from massive bases. The blades curve inward and meet high above the roadway, making a sharp silhouette against Baghdad’s pale sky. Wide asphalt, concrete edges and formal open space emphasize their scale; passing cars look small beneath them. In strong midday sun, the metal catches bright highlights and the hands cast hard shadows. Traffic and wind replace the quieter sounds of a pedestrian monument.

The Iraqi Museum stands in Baghdad’s Alawi area behind a broad, pale stone-and-concrete frontage and a formal entrance marked المتحف العراقي. Outside, visitors pass gates and security checks from busy streets into quieter museum grounds. Inside, long galleries hold carved stone reliefs, statues, clay tablets and pottery, with Arabic and English labels beside display cases. Large ancient sculptures occupy substantial floor space; smaller objects sit behind glass under controlled lighting. Shoes make soft taps on hard floors, while conversation stays low. Baghdad’s bright daylight falls sharply across the entrance, contrasting with the subdued, even light around the exhibits.

The University of Baghdad’s main campus occupies a large site at Al-Jadriya, where the Tigris bends around southern Baghdad. Low modernist academic buildings, pale concrete surfaces, shaded walkways and open planted spaces sit behind campus gates marked جامعة بغداد. Students cross between faculties carrying backpacks and folders; groups pause under palms or near building entrances. Arabic notices appear alongside English academic text. Cars and buses approach on the surrounding roads, while footsteps and conversation fill the internal paths. In summer the light is intense and shadows under the covered passages are crisp; dust softens more distant views.

Baghdad International Airport lies west of central Baghdad, reached by a long airport road and controlled entrances. Low terminal buildings combine pale cladding, glass doors and wide forecourts; signs read مطار بغداد الدولي alongside English directions. Inside, travellers move past check-in counters with wheeled suitcases, while luggage carts rattle over hard floors and announcements echo overhead. Outside the windows, aircraft taxi slowly between aprons and runways, their engines rising from a distant whine to a heavy roar. Sunlight is strong on the concrete, often under a hazy beige sky; the terminal interior is cooler and evenly lit.

Sami Abdulrahman Park is a broad landscaped park in Erbil, with long walking paths, lawns, rows of trees, water features and open space for families. Kurdish signs mark paths and entrances, and the city’s buildings remain visible beyond the greenery. Walkers and joggers follow the paved loops while children use play areas; voices, bicycle wheels and fountain water give the park its softer sound. Summer afternoons are bright and dry, with people gathering under trees or returning in the cooler evening. Path lights come on after dusk, outlining the walks as families continue to stroll.

Family Mall is a large shopping complex on Erbil’s 100 Meter Road, with broad glass entrances, pale exterior panels and prominent Family Mall lettering. Cars pull into wide parking areas while families pass through sliding doors into bright corridors with polished floors, shopfront glass, escalators and food counters. Outside, traffic moves steadily on the divided road; inside, footsteps, children’s voices and overlapping conversations echo under even electric light. People wear jeans and shirts, long dresses, headscarves or Kurdish clothing. Kurdish speakers may greet someone with “سڵاو، چۆنی؟” and address a man as “کاکە”; Arabic speakers also use “السلام عليكم”.

Goizha rises immediately above Sulaymaniyah, its steep slopes showing pale brown rock, loose gravel and sparse grass that greens after rain. A winding paved road climbs past roadside viewpoints; from the higher bends, the city spreads below in dense blocks against a ring of mountains. Afternoon sun casts long shadows into gullies, while evening brings cooler air and a scatter of city lights. Wind brushes dry plants and carries faint traffic sounds up the slope. Visitors stop beside parked cars to take photographs, wearing casual clothes, coats in cold months or Kurdish dress. A common greeting is “سڵاو، چۆنی؟”; “کاکە” is a familiar respectful address for a man.

The central Sulaymaniyah bazaar is a tight network of covered passages and busy streets around Sara Square and Mawlawi Street. Small shops pack clothing, fabric, sweets, spices and household goods beneath signs in Kurdish and Arabic. Shutters, hanging merchandise and awnings narrow the view; fluorescent shop light meets daylight at each opening. Shoppers move around handcarts, and the sounds of bargaining, footsteps and traffic overlap. Men and women wear everyday jackets, dresses and headscarves, with Kurdish clothing also visible. Shopkeepers greet customers with “سڵاو، بەخێربێن” and may address a man as “کاکە”; Arabic-speaking visitors may say “السلام عليكم”.

Basra’s Corniche runs beside the broad Shatt al-Arab, where brown-green water ripples against embankments and the wakes of small boats spread outward. Date palms, railings and seating frame views of working river traffic and the opposite bank. Walkers gather toward sunset, when low golden light catches the water; in summer, the air remains hot and humid after dark. Engines, horns and conversations mingle with water slapping boat hulls. Families wear casual clothes, long dresses and headscarves, and vendors may sell tea or snacks. A greeting is “هلا بيك” or “السلام عليكم”; friends ask “شلونك؟” as they meet along the promenade.

Ashar is a crowded older commercial district of Basra, with narrow shop-lined streets opening onto busier roads. Look for weathered brick and plaster buildings beside newer concrete fronts; surviving traditional houses have projecting wooden shanasheel, their closely spaced slats shading windows above the street. Arabic shop signs, electrical cables, awnings and stacked goods fill the view. Pedestrians thread between parked cars, carts and slow traffic while sellers call out over engines and footsteps. Sunlight strikes upper facades but leaves passages in patchy shade; summer air is hot and humid. People wear everyday shirts, dishdashas, dresses and headscarves. “هلا بيك” and “شلونك؟” are natural local greetings.

Sindbad Island is a low island in Basra’s Shatt al-Arab, surrounded by broad, slow-moving brown-green water. From the bank, palms and other greenery break its level outline, with river craft passing nearby. Its leisure structures and paths can show differing degrees of upkeep, so avoid depicting a uniformly new resort or assuming every attraction is operating. A boat’s wake rocks smaller craft, water taps at hulls, and engines carry across the river. Light is sharp on clear days and softens to amber near sunset; summers are hot and humid. Visitors in casual clothes may greet one another with “هلا بيك” or “السلام عليكم”.

Karbala’s old city centers on the shrines of Imam Husayn and al-Abbas, joined by the broad pedestrian space of Bayn al-Haramayn. Gold-colored domes and minarets rise above tiled gates, arcades, marble paving and surrounding streets of hotels and shops. Arabic signs advertise food, lodging and religious goods. Pilgrims walk steadily in groups, often in black clothing; some carry small bags, and footwear is removed before entering shrine interiors. Footsteps and conversation fill the open space, with recitation audible near the shrines. Sun makes the pale paving bright, while night lighting outlines the architecture. Visitors commonly say “السلام عليكم” and address another pilgrim as “يا زائر”.

topic: Najaf old city and the Wadi al-Salam cemetery
body: Najaf’s old city has narrow lanes and crowded shopfronts leading toward the shrine of Imam Ali, whose gold-colored dome and minarets rise above its walls. Nearby, Wadi al-Salam extends across a vast area of sandy lanes and densely placed graves: upright inscribed stones, low masonry tombs and small built chambers in uneven rows. Arabic names and verses appear on markers. Visitors walk carefully between graves; the sounds are footsteps, quiet conversation and distant traffic. Strong sun gives stone and dust a pale beige glare, while shrine lighting warms the streets after dark. Dress is generally modest, and people greet one another with “السلام عليكم”.

Low, flat-roofed houses of plastered brick and concrete sit behind reed fences and narrow dirt lanes. Date palms rise above small vegetable plots; irrigation channels carry river water between the fields. The broad Tigris or Euphrates moves slowly past muddy banks, where a narrow wooden boat rocks gently against its rope. In summer, hard sunlight bleaches the walls and throws short palm shadows; winter brings softer light and damp ground. Men in dishdashas or everyday shirts, and women in long dresses or abayas, walk between homes. Water laps, palm fronds rustle, and distant motor pumps hum.

A two-lane asphalt road cuts through flat beige gravel and sparse scrub, its edges dusty and uneven. At the checkpoint, concrete T-walls and plastic barriers guide vehicles into a slow, curved lane beneath a simple shade canopy. Arabic signs instruct drivers to reduce speed; a small booth has tinted windows, a desk and a wall-mounted fan. Uniformed personnel speak briefly with drivers while trucks idle behind taxis and private cars. Heat shimmer wavers above the road in bright afternoon sun, and fine dust lifts behind passing tyres. Engines rumble, air brakes hiss, and voices carry across the open ground.

Concrete and pale-stone teaching blocks frame paved walkways, planted courtyards and small lawns. Arabic signs identify colleges, departments and lecture halls; noticeboards carry exam schedules and student announcements. Groups of students cross between buildings with backpacks, folders and paper cups of tea. Clothing varies from jeans and shirts to long skirts, headscarves and dishdashas. In strong midday light, covered corridors make sharp bands of shade across the paving. A campus bus pulls up slowly, its doors folding open; shoes tap on tile, conversations overlap in Iraqi Arabic, and a distant lecture drifts through an open classroom window.

Small tables stand close together beneath ceiling fans, with plastic or wooden chairs facing the street and a television mounted high on the wall. Glasses of dark amber tea arrive on saucers with little spoons and sugar; a kettle steams near the counter. Men of different ages talk, watch football or play dominoes, placing each tile with a crisp click. Some wear dishdashas, others shirts and trousers. Daylight enters through the open frontage, leaving the back of the room dimmer under fluorescent tubes. Traffic and vendor calls mix with clinking glasses, fan noise and the hiss of boiling water.

A tiled living room has light-painted walls, a patterned rug and upholstered sofas arranged around the edges, leaving open floor space for visitors. A low table holds small tea glasses, a tissue box and a plate of dates or biscuits. Curtains soften the sun from a courtyard-facing window; a ceiling fan turns steadily above an air conditioner. Family photographs or framed Arabic calligraphy may hang over a side cabinet. Relatives in everyday clothes sit together while someone carries in a tray, the glasses trembling slightly as it moves. Conversation, a television in the next room and the rattle of a spoon fill the house.

A raised stage anchors a broad hall of round tables, banquet chairs and glossy tiled flooring. Fabric drapes, flowers and warm LED strips frame the couple’s seats; lighting shifts colour across the dance floor. Guests arrive in suits, formal dresses, abayas and other occasion wear, depending on the family and the event. Servers carry trays between tightly spaced tables while children weave carefully past the chairs. When music starts, groups step and clap in rhythm, and dresses sway as people turn. Amplified Iraqi songs and the sharp beat of a drum fill the room, followed by applause and overlapping congratulations.

Polished floor tiles reflect bright ceiling panels and illuminated shopfronts along wide, air-conditioned corridors. Arabic and English signs mark clothing stores, phone shops, cafés and the food court. Escalator steps rise at a steady pace behind glass balustrades; shoppers wait at the landing with bags and pushchairs. Families and groups of friends wear a mix of casual clothes, headscarves, abayas and dishdashas. Through the entrance glass, strong daylight contrasts with the cool interior light. Footsteps squeak on tile, shop music overlaps softly, and café cups clink beneath the continuous hum of ventilation.

A hospital ward has pale washable walls, a tiled floor and beds spaced beside narrow bedside cabinets. White sheets cover the mattresses; privacy curtains hang from ceiling tracks, and oxygen outlets and call buttons sit above some headboards. Arabic labels identify rooms and nursing stations. Nurses in scrubs move between beds, checking charts and speaking quietly with patients and relatives. Fluorescent lights give an even glow, while daylight from high windows brightens one side of the room. Wheeled trolleys roll with a faint rattle, air conditioning hums, and a monitor occasionally sounds a short electronic beep.

An Iraqi government office often has a concrete or pale-stone exterior, an Arabic sign naming the ministry or directorate, and an Iraqi flag above the entrance: horizontal red, white, and black stripes with green «الله أكبر» centered on the white stripe. Inside, fluorescent light falls on tiled floors, metal filing cabinets, stamped paper forms, and desks with computers and document trays. Visitors wait on plastic or upholstered chairs, then approach a service window or desk when called. Staff may wear shirts and trousers, abayas, or headscarves. Footsteps, low conversation, printers, and the thud of a stamp fill the room; visitors greet staff with «السلام عليكم».

In an Iraqi public-school classroom, rows of shared wooden or metal-framed desks face a whiteboard or chalkboard. Arabic writing, arithmetic exercises, and sometimes a map hang against painted plaster walls. Tall windows admit strong daylight, often softened by curtains; ceiling fans turn above students’ notebooks and schoolbags. Pupils commonly wear school uniforms, though colours and rules vary by school. A teacher writes at the board, then walks between desks as pupils raise their hands or read aloud. Chairs scrape tile or terrazzo, pages rustle, and the fan hums. Students may greet the teacher with «السلام عليكم أستاذ» or «أستاذة».

Basra International Stadium stands within Basra Sports City, with a broad oval bowl and an exterior of tall, pale structural ribs evoking palm trunks. Its pitch is vivid green beneath banks of seating for roughly 65,000 spectators; floodlights brighten the grass against the dark evening sky. Fans in team shirts and Iraqi-flag colours stream through concourses, wave scarves, and chant in Arabic. The Iraqi flag has horizontal red, white, and black stripes, with green «الله أكبر» on the white stripe. On the pitch, players sprint, turn, and send the ball skimming or bouncing across the grass. Whistles cut through layered cheers, clapping, and drumbeats.
